author: Ryan Hermenet
title: Climate activists concerned with newly approved state energy project - NewsBreak
text:
By Ryan Hermenet ,
1 hours ago ROCHESTER, N.Y. (WROC) — After a year of back and forth between a major natural gas power plant in the Finger Lakes and officials with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), an agreement has been reached which will allow the facility to continue operations. But many climate activists worry about the repercussions the settlement could lead to.
Greenridge Generation LLC, based in Dresden, N.Y. along Seneca Lake, filed a lawsuit against the state in 2024 after the DEC denied its air permit renewal application. The new agreement grants the permit to the company, valid for the next five years.
Some say the agreement puts the best interest of New Yorkers aside, including Lieutenant Governor Antonio Delgado.
“Allowing this plant to continue operating undermines the law, weakens public trust and tells every other polluter that the rule of law is indeed optional,” Delgado said.
In contrast, Governor Kathy Hochul has expressed her open support for the agreement. She says the plant’s continued operations in the Finger Lakes will contribute to lower utility rates for state residents and attract major economic projects to the region.
Delgado explained why he believes there to be much more at stake within this issue.
“It’s not just about emissions targets,” Delgado said. “It’s about moral responsibility, it’s about whether our children inherit a state that has the courage to stand up for what’s right: a planet in which they can actually breathe clean air.”
Delgado further referenced the targets outlined in the 2019 Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act . One condition of the law is for greenhouse gas emissions to be reduced by at least 40% below the state’s 1990 emissions levels by 2030.
Co-Founder and Vice President of the Seneca Lake Guardian Yvonne Taylor said she worries this agreement will stray the state further from this goal.
“[Greenridge] pumps nearly half a million tons of carbon dioxide into our air every year, undoing the progress so many fought for under New York’s climate act,” Taylor said.
For many of these clean energy advocates, the fear of increased pollution extends to fears of decreased tourism in the Finger Lakes and a lower quality of life for those who live near Seneca Lake.
Mike Penn, who owns Ria’s Wines along Seneca Lake, shared why this is a major concern for him.
“People come here because of the lake’s beauty, it’s clean air and our world-class food and wine,” Penn said. “If we let a private crypto mining company degrade these, we’re risking the very foundation of our regional economy.
